correctness.rationale: With \(A=a+1\), \(M=2^A-1\), one has \(\tau=2A\) and \(\sigma=M(p+1)\). Cohen's prime-support and valuation criterion plus LTE shows every prime divisor of \(M\) must be \(p\), so \(M=p^c\). A multiplicative-order argument then forces \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=A\). Any odd prime dividing \(p+1\) would divide both \(A\) and \(p-1\), impossible, so \(p+1\) is a power of two; primality forces the Mersenne exponent to equal \(A\), hence \(c=1\). The converse is the standard even-perfect identity. A fresh brute-force defining-condition replay for \(a\le12\) and odd primes through 2000 found only \((a,p)=(1,3),(2,7),(4,31),(6,127)\), all with index one.
risks: The proof depends essentially on the odd part occurring to the first power; extra odd-prime exponent factors change \(\tau(n)\).

value.rationale: This is a natural infinite structural slice of an explicitly identified two-prime superharmonic classification problem. It connects the superharmonic condition sharply back to the Euclid–Euler even-perfect family and determines the exact index.

final_claim: For \(a\ge1\) and odd prime \(p\), the number \(2^a p\) is superharmonic if and only if \(a+1\) is prime and \(p=2^{a+1}-1\) is prime; equivalently this squarefree-odd-part two-prime slice consists exactly of even perfect numbers and has superharmonic index one.
limitations: Odd part is one prime to the first power.
No claim for odd superharmonic numbers or general two-prime exponents.
